chunks: The others among the Companions said: this report is abrogated. Had the two groups not regarded this wording as preventing the obligation of ghusl without ejaculation, those who denied the obligation of ghusl would not have argued by means of the report, nor would the others have claimed its abrogation.

Then the Shaykh, may Allah the Exalted support him, said: whoever performs wudu (ablution) while there is a ring on his hand, let him turn it or move it when washing his hand so that the water may reach beneath it. Likewise is the woman, if she has a bracelet on her arm, up to his statement: and whatever falls from the water does not harm the one performing wudu (ablution).
That is indicated by the following.

key_terms.اَلْغُسْلِ: ghusl (ritual bath); the major purification under discussion
key_terms.اَلْمَاءِ: water; the purifying substance whose reach is legally relevant
key_terms.تَوَضَّأَ: performed wudu (ablution); entered the act of ritual washing
key_terms.خَاتَمٌ: ring; an object that may block water from reaching the skin
key_terms.سِوَارٌ: bracelet; similarly treated in the ruling of wudu (ablution)
key_terms.مَنْسُوخٌ: abrogated; no longer legally operative according to those cited
key_terms.وُجُوبِ: obligation; legal requirement in juristic discussion

ai.seo_question: Does a ring or bracelet need to be moved during wudu (ablution), and how was the hadith of ghusl understood by the Companions?
ai.summary: This passage discusses a juristic disagreement over a report concerning the obligation of ghusl, including the claim that the report was abrogated. It then shifts to a practical legal ruling in wudu (ablution), stating that a ring or bracelet should be moved so that water reaches beneath it, and that water falling during wudu (ablution) does not invalidate it.
